utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This morning we have resumed to hear submissions from the Defence under the provisions of Rule 98 bis. I see you are at full strength, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I wouldn't have it any other way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I may not be, but we'll carry on. So, Mr. Tapuskovic, we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. By taking the floor, I'm fully aware of the possibilities and the authority that the Trial Chamber has at the moment under Rule 98 bis. I will do my best to be as concise as possible and even try not to use up all the time allocated to me. I will be very careful, which is probably against my nature, because I can deliver my speech in about 20 minutes, but I will take due care in order to enable the interpreters to translate everything I say. I will make a effort to focus only on the most important issues that I believe the Defence, at this juncture, should try and explain. As I said, I'm fully aware, according to the previous practice of this Tribunal that at this stage of the proceedings, the Trial Chamber cannot evaluate the credibility and credence of the witnesses and the weight or weaknesses of evidence with regard to specific counts in the indictment, especially not with regard to the incidents discussed here. I'm not going to deal at all with the incidents, nor seek that you evaluate anything with regard to these incidents because this is simply impossible. If I dealt with one single incident only, I would use up the whole time allocated it me today. For instance, I cannot seek your response today to the question how it was possible for a modified air bomb to explode without leaving any shrapnel or what kind of shells can fly in without being heard or seen. I'm not going to talk about these things in my submission today. The 98 bis requirement, as I understand the practice of this Tribunal, can be met or successful, unless there is no evidence corroborating specific counts of -- in the indictment, or if the evidence lacks any credulity in order to support the conviction in a proper way, even if the evidence is taken in the most favourable light by the Prosecution. Today, I'm going to be mainly focussing on only one question. I'm going to raise this question, although I am aware that in view of the limited points of 98 bis rule the Trial Chamber could probably not make a ruling today. This question refers to the question whether the Prosecution has provided enough evidence supporting the main act of perpetration in the indictment dominating all counts in the indictment, and from which all other crimes stem that the accused Dragomir Milosevic has been accused under Count 1, under Counts 2 to 4, and Counts 5 to 7. This crucial element and allegation stating that Dragomir Milosevic in the period between 10th of August -- 10th of April, 1994 and 21st November, 1995 conducted an extensive campaign of shelling and sniping upon civilian areas in civilian population of Sarajevo, and that this campaign was the one and only thing that was on the mind of the accused Dragomir Milosevic, and that it was a crucial act committed through his actions. I'm not going to talk about today whether there was an allegation or an order, in that respect, whether there was any meeting between Dragomir Milosevic and other persons on the subjects, did he talk about representatives of the international community about this issues. This is something for another occasion. What I want to point out today is that we should look whether there is sufficient evidence from all this involving terror, inhumane treatment, and violations of the laws and customs of war. Therefore, for that purpose, I have to give a history of the events in these proceedings. As you know, on the 18th of December, 2006, which is 15 days after the decision rendered in the Galic case by the Appeals Chamber and it was rendered on the 30th of November, 2006, the Prosecution amended the indictment but without changing the counts in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Tapuskovic, but I think you did say that the consideration is whether there is sufficient evidence. I'm looking for it in the transcript, but I heard it. Yes. I haven't found it, but I did hear the translation to the effect that the consideration was whether there is sufficient evidence and I paused. I'm just checking to see whether you did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In any event, I just wanted to clarify that the standard of the sufficiency of evidence was in the old Rule and that was changed in 2004, and now the judgement of acquittal will be entered on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. In my view, there is a difference between a search for sufficiency of evidence and a simpler quest to see whether there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. So that, as I understand it - and this would always have been the law, although perhaps not the practice - if there is some evidence capable of supporting a conviction, the submission under 98 bis will not succeed. So with that in mind, you may continue. Yes. It is page 2, line 18/19. The question refers to a question whether the Prosecution has provided, it says, "enough evidence," but it did come across to me as sufficient evidence supporting the main act. And it is in relation to that I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood you perfectly, Your Honours. Yes, that is a nuance; and in that respect, you have surely warned me in a proper way. In fact, what I wanted to say was that the campaign which involves something as an exclusive intention on the part of the accused is that the sole purpose was to jeopardise the lives of civilians, and the sole purpose was to target civilian targets. I will deal only with the fact that this does not stem literally from a single piece of evidence. Maybe I said there was insufficient evidence, but that is why I said at the beginning that I do not intend to deal with individual incidents, because all these incidents that the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, is suspected of and charged with stems from this campaign. However, this -- the existence of this campaign was not proved in a proper way by the Prosecution through a single piece of evidence. So this is my basic thesis at this stage. I know very well what are the capabilities and authorities of the Chamber when deciding according to Rule 98 bis. Believe me, if I am to deal with a single incident, the analysis thereof, since we were not able to do anything in writing, would require a lot of time, and will not make it possible for me to speak about the campaign that the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, is charged with and which is the source of everything else. I believe that the Trial Chamber can be satisfied with this explanation that I will give you and that I will be allowed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm trying to explain here is everything that took place and what we found out in the proceedings, documents, what we heard from witnesses, and the evidence introduced through these witnesses. That is why I wanted to start with the 18th of December, 2006, which is 15 days after the Appeals ruling in the Galic case, when the indictment was amended without changing the counts. I'm particularly referring to paragraph 19 in the indictment, which reads that: "From May 1992, when he was commander of the Romanija Infantry Brigade, and from July 1993 when he was the Chief of Staff, he knew of the campaign against the civilian population, that he inherited this campaign and continued its pursuit." So what did the Prosecution do? Less than a month before this trial began, the Prosecution expanded the consciousness of the accused to include the period before his tenure; that is to say, to all the 44 months of the campaign. In that way, we have been put in a situation when, at the moment, we didn't even know the scope of responsibility of the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, to be dealt with by the offence. Since counts in the indictment were not changed, there was no remedy at our disposal at the moment, and to seek probably some response by the Trial Chamber to our motion had we been able to file one. Moreover, on the 18th of December, 2006, the Prosecution submitted, on the same day, when they amended the indictment, a motion for a formal notice of facts under Rule 94(B), and it involved as many as 181 facts. In its brief, dated 21st of January --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the date of the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please repeat the date. The interpreter didn't have the date. Is it the 21st of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, my mistake. 25th of January, 2007. I said 2005. Yes, my mistake. In this submission, in this motion, the Prosecution claim that the facts under number 50 to 181 refer to the issues which were in dispute in the current proceedings. Furthermore, the Prosecution claimed that these proposed facts, although they do not refer to the indictment period, are of such notion that they prove paragraph 19 in the indictment stating that the accused conducted the campaign of sniping and shelling of the civilians, and that he knew about this campaign as far back as in May 1992. This position taken by the Prosecution clearly shows that they used these established facts in order to prove that the accused conducted the campaign and, furthermore, much more that he had known about the campaign in May 1992. Therefore, his responsibility, according to the Prosecution, should encompass the whole period of 44 months. However, the key issue is that through these established facts, the Prosecution wanted to prove that there was the existence of shelling and sniping campaign of civilian population as the only objective. When the Prosecution filed this motion, they said something different. In the motion dated the 25th, it also mentioned that the facts, 57 to 181, although they were relevant about the awareness, reiterate the same without saying directly anything about criminal responsibility of the accused and his mens rea. The Defence's understanding is that in this way of trying to prove a key fact is absolutely inappropriate and cannot constitute evidence of the existence of the campaign contained in the indictment. Supposedly, the Prosecution should have taken a different course. They should have tried to prove the existence of this campaign in the period relevant for Dragomir Milosevic and to provide evidence that Dragomir Milosevic, throughout the indictment period, without any military purpose, first, I'll give you a couple of examples: An extensive shelling and sniping of exclusively civilian targets; that throughout the indictment period there was a extensive and widespread campaign on a large scale involving a large number of casualties; that throughout the period, the frequency and geographical dispersion of this campaign was in existence; and that throughout the whole period, the campaign was based on territorial and topographic advantages and particularly superiority in terms of weapons and ammunition; that these incidents were evenly distributed throughout the period; that the civilian casualties were also eventually distributed throughout the period of the document; and so on and so forth. All of this put forth as something being totally out of any military context. The Prosecution didn't even make an endeavour to prove any of these allegations. They just listed these facts established in the Galic case without feeling the need to prove any of the elements dealt with the Appeals Chamber in the Galic case. Instead of providing evidence to corroborate these facts, the Prosecution's point of departure was what he knew at the time before he became what he became, and they took the course of providing evidence of a number of sniping incidents and a number of shelling incidents, as stipulated in paragraph 29. Furthermore - and that is the reason why I didn't want to address these issues - even the few incidents described here, whether they involved a sniping or shelling as the basis of a crime, should be, must be subjected to very serious criticism. I didn't have enough time to prove that the largest number of these incidents still remain unproved beyond reasonable doubt. Not even the crime base was sufficiently established with a sufficient number of cases in the relevant period, and the campaign alone was not proven at all beyond stipulating certain facts stating that Dragomir Milosevic merely inherited the campaign once he was appointed commander. We've heard a number of victims, and most of the witnesses we heard, I believe almost 20 or 25, were policemen, boys, young boys who were in charge of those investigations. We only saw two officers, military officers; a commander and an officer, and they tried to portray a civilian society being targeted by an army for no reason at all, as if there were no belligerent parties present in the area. In the first instance judgement in Galic, it also stated that the Sarajevo front was the central theatre of all events in Sarajevo; whereby, here the OTP attempted to prove that this was a civilian area with a certain number of soldiers targeted by a very strong army which enjoyed superiority for no reason at all with the sole intent of doing nothing but that. There is another thing I must say, and that is that the -- the adjudicated facts in that case are irrelevant concerning the criminal responsibility of Dragomir Milosevic, since none of those facts can be used in order to prove the mens rea, the acts, and behaviour of the accused. I'm looking for a reference. I believe it was in the court ruling of the 10th of April, whereby, something was stated. I will try to find that reference. It is stated that he must have known of the existence of the campaign, and that he should have taken steps to prevent such crimes from happening again and to punish the perpetrators as least of the moment when he was pointed commander. If one allows for such reasoning, then we -- then we need not be here. There is no room for this trial because it seems we have the facts, and we need the incidents only in order to come up with a judgement; then one must ask: What is the sense of it all, Unless sufficient evidence was provided as to the existence of the campaign? As I said at the initial stages of the proceedings, concerning the amended indictment and the application for judicial notice of adjudicated facts, before that, we didn't know what the scope of the case was. And since we still have no final ruling of the Court as for the fate of those adjudicated facts, whether all of them will be taken into account or not, we find ourselves in a position that two weeks before we are to forward our witness list - and I may freely say so - we still do not know the scope of responsibility of the accused. It is a very good question as to what preparation we can indeed carry out. We will meet all of the deadlines and rulings made by the Court, but we find ourselves in a tight spot, since we still don't know the scope of responsibility of the accused Dragomir Milosevic. It turns out that he is to stand -- to be held responsible for the period when he was commander and also when Stanislav Galic was commander, and that he should bear the blame for both with an appropriate sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to take as little time as possible to complete my submissions, but there is another thing I needed to say. What is particularly striking here, and even basic criminal law knowledge and some common sense would find that striking, and that pertains to some basic criminal responsibility features. I have dealt with criminal law throughout my career, and I feel obliged and invited to say a few things on that topic. Can one inherit criminal responsibility, as envisaged in Article 7 of the Statute of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. What sort of criminal responsibility is it when it allows for a possibility to state something of that kind, that one can inherit criminal responsibility? It is beyond dispute between the parties here that, if I may say so, General Dragomir Milosevic inherited the position, the military position of his predecessor, this being General Galic. But that is all he inherited. As for his acts and behaviour, it can only be viewed within his state of mind and the mens rea, as it is referred to in this Tribunal, only during the period that he is to be held responsible; that is, for the time that he was charged with in the indictment. This is not a matter of inheritance. One cannot the inherit such a thing. This is criminal responsibility which can be seen only within the relevant time in the indictment and only for the acts and mens rea in that period. No inheritance factor exists in criminal law. Responsibility is only attributed to a certain period of time pertaining to me and me alone. Everything I want to say about the campaign today has to do with these few basic matters that I have mentioned. Even if he had known of certain things from the preceding period, his behaviour has only to do with the time when he was in the position of authority; and only during that period, one can try to establish what his liability was. It is one of the most notorious facts when it comes to criminal responsible, an individual responsibility under Article 7 of the Statute, and it can be viewed in no other way. In order to make myself even clearer regarding that, I will try to use an example, although some may find it in bad taste, but I don't see why not. I can mention a quote from the dissenting opinion of Judge Nieto-Navia, when this Judge forwarded a separate and dissenting opinion as to the responsibility of General Galic. Concerning the existing campaign, this Judge stated that based on the evidence in the relevant period, one may not conclude that the SRK intentionally carried out a sniping campaign against civilians. There is another thing that was also present in this case, in my view, and that was a portion of that opinion that I wanted to quote. This Judge determined that there was no existence of such a campaign, that it cannot be determined. The Judge said that after the explosion at the Markale market on the 5th of February, 1994, an agreement was put in place of excluding all heavy weaponry from any use in the city. The area of total exclusion was established. Based on that fact, on the existence of the exclusion zone between February and August of that year, he believed that it is sufficient to show that in the period that Galic was accused with committing crimes, one cannot conclude that the campaign existed throughout. This fact is not in dispute, I believe, because the zone of total exclusion, during the period when Dragomir Milosevic was commander, existed throughout, absolutely so. It is but one fact, and I will not go into any others for the time being. I will mention them, however, when I give my opening statement. But this factor alone shows that such a campaign could not have been in existence throughout the period when Dragomir Milosevic was in command. I will address yet some other things at a later stage. The Prosecutor and the Prosecution in this proceeding brought a historian before this Bench. It was Robert Donia. He produced a report based on some historical background and political and military context. As he states in the introduction, "My report will focus on the period between November 1994 and August 1995; that is, within the period encompassed by the indictment against General Dragomir Milosevic." Even that evidence encompassed only the period until August 1994. It was held against me in this Court that I indulge in history far too often. Your Honours, as for a historical background in the case of Dragomir Milosevic, I don't want to go into it at all, or I wouldn't have, had it not been opened here in the report. I had to present my objections to that report and to cross-examine the witness. As for this case, I do not believe that the historical or political background is important. It was towards the end of the war, and I have no reason to go into that for that reason alone. However, the military context throughout the case period was of such a nature that it should have been the only relevant thing for any possibly decisions of yours, particularly when it comes to the sniping and shelling campaign allegation. For without that military context, which was clearly evident, one cannot decide on anything in this case. However, all the evidence and facts presented did not provide for sufficient military context. I will try to be very brief by way of example. If we take W-156 in English, it is page 46 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In the B/C/S, it is page 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to interrupt counsel's submissions. However, if we are going to talk this witness's testimony, I think out of an abundance of caution, we should go into private session. This witness testified in closed session; and until we resolve what could be made public, if anything, from his testimony and what could not, I think at this stage, we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Are you saying something in response to the submissions just made?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to read one sentence which will not endanger anyone. The only thing I said was W-156. Apart from that, no identity is known, and this one sentence will not reveal it. There is no need to go into private session when this is but a quote which can describe the context that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without the military context, which was not mentioned in the indictment, one cannot view or assess the responsibility of the accused for the things he was charged with. In that regard, the Prosecutor did not attempt to prove anything. What we have is the dominant presence of the adjudicated facts in order to corroborate certain incidents, and no proof or evidence is offered for the things that I mentioned. Perhaps I can draw a parallel, a comparison with the indictment to support my argument. What you can see is that in the indictment, when it refers to the incidents, by the incidents alone, one cannot see that the incident -- that the number of incidents or their intensity could testify as to the existence of a campaign. Not even the number of victims can support that claim. Even on cursory reading of the indictment, one could find that because, according to the document, there were four phases: First, the phases after the anti-sniping agreement until the end of 1994; then we have the phase of cease-fire between January and May 1995; then we have the phase of General offensive of the ABiH; and then NATO air-strikes. If one is to compare only that with what he is charged with, with minimum analysis of the indictment, one can see that the Prosecutor was completely unable to prove that the campaign was in existence throughout the period, the campaign of targeting solely civilians and civilian targets. We can compare that to the contents of P602, this being the police report. Perhaps I needn't go into detail; but it is clear that in the period between August and December 1994, there were wounded but there were only nine people killed, and there was a very small number of incidents. Between early January and May, if we take that as a piece of information - and I believe this is how you adopted the evidence - there were only two killed and but a few incidents. Most of the incidents happened between May and August when there was a general offensive on the part of the ABiH against or at all front lines. This is the period when we have most of the victims; and, of course, subsequently, most of the civilians that could have been killed were killed in that particular period. The only way to avoid that would have been to a complete surrender of the army of Republika Srpska. In the last period, as of late August until November, even according to the indictment, there was not a single stated incident but there were one or two victims. For such a complain as they claim that was in existence, the Prosecutor did not provide a single piece of evidence. That campaign is the basis for all other crimes mentioned in the indictment. This is what I wanted to present to you. Finally, I would like to say something about how informed the accused was. It may sound a little by the absurd to say that in May, or rather, from the beginning of the conflict he knew about that and he inherited that. Please. The Galic judgement was rendered on the 30th of November, 2006. Up until then, Galic was innocent, and it was not known what he was going to be charged with and what happened during his era. So what is the point, then, at all to mention that the accused knew something, and that this should dominate this whole proceedings. It is beyond doubt that he learned about this. It may also sound absurd on the date when the second instance judgement was rendered, and even if he did know, it is impossible to establish any inherited responsibility. In order not to be repetitive and not to tire you, in view of all that, the campaign of targeting civilians and civilian target has not been established on the basis of a single piece of evidence. I think this the only thing that have I to impart on you at this juncture because I'm not going to address any other issues today. Time will come for me to tackle these issues in my opening statement and my closing statement as well. This fact, in my view, has not been proved at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I'm going to do is ask for some guidance from the Trial Chamber, first of all, and then I think I will ask if we have a ten-minute break so that we can kind of get our approach in order, because we had prepared a certain approach. I think we may adjust it, based on what we heard today. We were prepared to go through every single incident and talk about every single incident in the indictment based on the submission of Defence counsel. Although he challenged the campaign and although the specific incidents are, of course, relevant to the campaign, because he did not specifically challenge the scheduled incidents, I'm not inclined to go into those, unless Your Honours ask me to. In which case, we're perfectly prepared to do. We're ready, we will go through it, and we will do it. But that is the point of guidance that -- and if Your Honours are unsure, then perhaps we should do it. But if Your Honours think there is no need to go through each incident, then we'll save the time and focus on other issues that have been raised by Defence counsel and that are raised in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecution response must be prompted, not only by the submissions the Defence has made, but by the law of the Tribunal. What is required? What is the standard? That is what you should have in mind. I said to Mr. Tapuskovic what my understanding of the law is, and I don't see how it would become necessary to go into all the incidents. What we are looking for at this stage is whether there is some evidence capable of supporting a conviction on the counts in the indictment, and I would expect the Prosecution, in its response, to provide an indication of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Could we have just a ten-minute break? I think we can shorten dramatically our presentation if we do that. We have divided up the presentation. It's not just me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is not necessary. I don't believe that that is necessary at all. It would show that you do not understand the 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So you just want us to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, my learned colleagues feel, notwithstanding what I have said, if you wish to have a short break, you are entitled to it. So we will give you a short break of ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think it will be to the benefit of everyone. Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.58 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm going to first briefly respond to a few points made by Defence counsel, then I will give a brief introduction; and then, as I indicated, we have divided up our presentation, and others will speak and then I will speak at the end. We have, during the break, shortened dramatically what we have planned to do. Defence counsel repeatedly suggested that the burden on the Prosecution is to prove that the sole purpose of the military campaign, of the campaign of the SRK, that its sole purpose, its objective, exclusive objective was to target civilians. And that suggestion was made repeatedly in the submission of the Defence. That submission misstates both the law and the facts in this case. The law, it is quite clear, does not require a -- that the Prosecution prove with respect to the terror count in Count 1 or any of the other Counts that the sole objective of the accused was to target civilians or was to cause terror. And with respect to terror in particular, because I take it that this is really what the Defence counsel was addressing, I would point the Trial Chamber to the Galic Appeal Judgement at paragraphs 99 to 104, specifically paragraph 104, which explicitly states that the Prosecution need not prove that is the sole objective, only that is a primary objective. Secondly, it has never been the Prosecution's case, nor do we believe it is the evidence, that there was only targeting of civilian objects during the indictment period. Of course, there was a -- there was military activity. There was military fighting going on during that time-period, and we accept that. In fact, we have led evidence about that, specifically, from the very start of the trial to the very end. However, that evidence and that position is not inconsistent with our position that, at the same time, there was a widespread and systematic campaign of shelling and sniping of civilian objects by the SRK under the command of the accused during the indictment period, which had as one of its primary purposes to cause terror. Therefore, we believe that the facts support every -- that the evidence and the facts support every element of every count charged in this indictment. Secondly, [sic] in Defence counsel's submission, there was a suggestion that the indictment is supported only by the scheduled incidents, or that the allegations of a campaign are supported only by the scheduled incidents. That, of course, is not the case. As is explicitly stated in the indictment, and has always been our position, the scheduled incidents are illustrative. They form illustrations of the campaign. There is, however, other evidence, significant evidence, necessary evidence, in the case of the campaign. The evidence of the campaign of shelling and sniping and of terror is supported by the scheduled incidents, by evidence of unscheduled incidents, and by other general evidence of witnesses and documents showing that throughout the indictment period, there existed a campaign of shelling and sniping of civilian objects. It is critical that the proof of the campaign depends on different types of evidence of the sort I have just mentioned, not simply the scheduled incidents. Third, and finally, in response to Defence counsel, there was considerable discussion about the adjudicated facts, which to us came as a by the of a surprise, since the present posture is that many of the adjudicated facts proposed by Prosecution are not part of the record, because by decision of the Trial Chamber, they were not accepted. Of course, that is still an open matter. But as the record currently stands, they are not part of the record. It baffles me a little bit why Defence counsel is arguing against them. However, just to make a few things clear, in case there is a confusion. Number one, it is, of course, not our case that the accused would be held responsible by virtue of the adjudicated facts were they to be admitted for the period before he became commander. The indictment is quite clear in the period that is charged against the accused, and that is not in any way changed by the adjudicated facts. The adjudicated facts and critically other evidence which is similar to the adjudicated facts and which has been led in this trial and which may, and we submit should be considered by the Trial Chamber, concerning the earlier time period is evidence. It evidence. It does not expand the liability of the accused. It is evidence concerning his knowledge during the time-period in which he is charged, and that's all it is. Now, I'm just going to talk very briefly about the 98 bis standard because, of course, the Trial Chamber has stated at the beginning of today's session what the standard is. And with respect to the standard, I would make just two points. The first is, as the Trial Chamber stated, the standard is if there is some evidence capable of supporting a conviction on each count, in making that determination, we submit that the law is - and here I am referring to the Kordic and Cerkez decision of the 6th of April 2000 - that all inferences should be drawn in favour of the Prosecution, and any alternative hypothesis by the Defence is at this stage to be disregarded. In other words, the Prosecution's case must be taken at its highest. The second point, and this I think is important to consider, is the effect of the change in the rule 98 bis that occurred in December of 2004. Your Honours have referred to one change in regard to the standard. However, there was another important change, and that is that the language of the removal changed from "charges" to "counts." Therefore, now the Trial Chamber need only consider each count and whether there is sufficient evidence regarding each count, not necessarily each allegation or each charge within a count. And the important ramification of that change for our case, we submit, is that, number one, the Trial Chamber need not consider every mode of liability alleged under each count. It is sufficient if the Trial Chamber finds that there is sufficient evidence for one mode of liability alleged under a count, that that count survives 98 bis. Secondly, it is not necessary for the Trial Chamber to consider every "crime base" allegation within a count; and with regards to our case, what we submit that means is that it is in fact not necessary for the Trial Chamber to look at every scheduled incident and determine with respect to every scheduled incident whether there is sufficient evidence regarding that scheduled incident. We submit, as we will argue later on, that there is; that is, for each one, there is sufficient evidence in fact. But the Chamber need not go into that detailed an analysis. It need only decide whether there is sufficient evidence to sustain the count. And, therefore, we submit sufficient evidence of perhaps enough scheduled incidents, unscheduled incidents, other types of evidence to support the counts with respect to each count in the indictment. The law for that approach has been adopted now in two Trial Chambers, and I believe in a third this week. And I would refer to the Mrksic Trial Chamber decision of the 3rd of July 2006, transcript reference 5959 to 5971; the Martic Trial Chamber decision of the 28th of June, 2006, at transcript 11311 -- I'm sorry those transcript pages were reversed. The second one was for Mrksic, and the first one was for Maric. This week, on the 1st of May, the parties in the Milutinovic case, which has started to argue the 98 bis, the parties agreed, both Defence and Prosecution, that this was the proper approach. Now, as I said, we have divided up the case. Mr. Docherty will briefly talk about the campaign of sniping. Mr. Waespi will talk about the campaign of shelling. Ms. Edgerton will talk about terror, and then I will talk at the end about command and control and about 7(3). We will not necessarily touch on every issue in the case; for example, we will not go on at length about armed conflict. I do not think there is a dispute with regards to the existence of an armed conflict during the relevant period. However, if there were, I would refer the Chamber to Mr. Harland's testimony at 322 to 326 which supports an armed conflict. Similarly, with respect to widespread and systematic, which is an element of some of the counts, we will not go into detail about that. However, all of the evidence taken together certainly establishes at this stage, and we submit evenly beyond a reasonable doubt, that there was a widespread and systematic campaign. As I said, we submit that every element on every count has been satisfied. We would ask, since we are trying to make this as quick as possible, though as comprehensive as possible, that if the Trial Chamber has a concern about any count, that it be raised with the Prosecution and we be permitted to address it if we have not done so already; because we believe that we should have an opportunity to be heard if there is a concern about any count. With that is correct, I will turn over the presentation to Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. Tapuskovic. The amended indictment charges the accused with sniping as murder in an Count 2 and as inhumane act in Count 3. Both Counts 2 and 3 are characterised as crimes against humanity. In addition, the accused is charged in Count 4 with sniping as a war crime, as unlawful attacks on civilians. There is evidence sufficient to support a conviction on each of these three counts and, therefore, the Defence submission that they should be dismissed ought itself to be dismissed. The existence of a sniping campaign directed against civilians in the Sarajevo area during the indictment period is supported, first of all, by the 12 scheduled incidents upon which the Prosecution has led evidence throughout this trial. Because the Defence has explicitly said that it forgoes at this stage a challenge to the evidence of those 12 incidents, I shall not spend time discussing them, unless the Trial Chambers has a specific question about any one of them. In which case, I will be happy to respond. The existence of the sniping campaign we first evidence of through the Prosecution's very first witness, Mr. David Harland, who said that "the basic dynamic of the conflict around Sarajevo was that the Serbs, who were in a militarily dominant position, would use sniping and shelling against civilians as a way to elicit Bosnian government behaviour they wanted." That is at page 324, lines 14 through 19. The concrete details of the implementation of this military strategy of this campaign of sniping against civilians were then fleshed out by witness after witness who have testified in this trial over and above the crime base witnesses who established the 12 scheduled incidents. Police officer Turkovic testified that during the war, calls for help on sniping and shelling came in from all over the city, all hours of the day and night, all times of the year. Page 5180, lines 9 through 17. 80 percent of his time, 80 per cent of his colleagues' time was taken up on these calls. Page 5179, 16 through 17, and 5180, 3 through 8. After the war, these calls dropped to zero. Page 5810, line 18. Exhibit Prosecution 602, a spreadsheet of police activity during the time of conflict, bears out that these calls were coming in at all hours and from all places. Witness Thorbjorn Overgard, an UNMO in Hrasnica, investigated sniping incidents in Hrasnica almost every day. "The origin of fire," he testified, "was always SRK territory, the victim always a civilian." It's transcript page 635, beginning at line 18 and continuing to transcript page 636, third line. The demographer, Ewa Tabeau, testified that even on militarily quiet days, civilians continued to be killed in violent, war-related ways, mostly through sniping. Protected witness, W-62, stated that going out to get food and water was dangerous due to sniping and shelling. Transcript page 882, lines 8 through 15. There was testimony that the victim of scheduled incident number 2, this was the shot from the school for the blind through the tunnel, was put into a private car rather than an ambulance to be transported to hospital to avoid sniper fire that they -- that the bystanders expected would be directed at an ambulance. That is page 887, line 20 continuing to page 888, line 9. Following scheduled incident number 2, this passageway became even more dangerous for the citizens of Sarajevo. Sniper fire was directed down it more frequently, despite the neighbourhood civilians hanging blankets as an anti-sniping barricade. And that is page 890, lines 3 through 16. A number of 92 ter statements introduced in this trial support the existence of a campaign through either scheduled incidents or general overview evidence. I direct the Court's attention to Prosecution Exhibit 92, in which a witness stated that she used to sleep with the blinds shut all the time for fear of sniping; Exhibit 95, in which a witness about a crime base incident, stating that earlier in the war, her husband had been hit in the cheek by a sniper's bullet that came through their apartment window. At page 1657, line 15, continuing to 1658, line 3, there was testimony from a Sarajevo tram driver that every intersection in town was dangerous to a tram driver. Canadian army officer Louis Fortin characterised sniping as a terrorist target and said that the targets were usually civilians but sometimes United Nations personnel. Page 484, line 22 to page 485, line 10. And he further testified that he personally was frequently sniped at while driving to Bosnia-Herzegovina command of UNPROFOR. Page 485, lines 11 through 13. With regard to sniping from Sharpstone into the north-east Sarajevo neighbourhood of Sedrenik, Nedzib Djozo of the police, the officer who responded to scheduled incident number ten, gave testimony that every day there was sniping into Sedrenik from Sharpstone and that many, many civilians - he used the figure of 100 as a synonym for a large number - were killed or wounded as a result of this fire. That's page 3695, at lines 12 through 18. Witness 54, testified that the assumption of every Sarajevo tram driver during the conflict was that when they took tram out, they would not come back. Page 1693, lines 6 through 13. Another witness, also a tram driver, testified that one might as well drive a tram as stay home, because staying home was dangerous. Indeed, the whole city was dangerous. Transcript page 1185, line 24 continuing to 1186, line 4. Also, as put by Witness Zecevic, at transcript 1637, lines 2 through 12, the Serbs "shot and fired at us and shelled us all the time." I would also refer the Trial Chamber respectively to Exhibit 541, the expert report Lieutenant Van der Weijden of the Dutch army, in which he stated, at pages 6 through 7, that he has visited the scene of every single scheduled sniping incident and evaluated it. And then when he testified, at transcript page 4287, line 2 through 9, he stated that in every single case, every single scheduled incident, fire should have been withheld because the victim could not have been positively identified as a combatant. In sum, Your Honours, the Prosecution has proven, has introduced extensive evidence, some of which I have mentioned here, some of which, such as the scheduled incidents, I have only adverted to, that there existed a campaign of sniping that was directed against the civilian population of Sarajevo during the indictment period, and that this campaign of sniping was widespread and systematic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Docherty. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. The amended indictment charges the accused with shelling as a murder, that is Count 5; shelling as an inhumane act, that is Count 6; and in count 7 also as an unlawful attacks on civilians. As my colleague Mr. Whiting already pointed out, the Prosecution has led evidence, presented evidence of three different categories in relation to the shelling campaign. There are the scheduled incidents 15; it's the unscheduled incidents, numerous numbers; and also evidence of a general nature or overview evidence. Briefly addressing them, first, these scheduled incident, the 15, which I won't go into in any detail, we have shown for each of them that they caused civilian casualties, death, injuries; that the origin of fire was from SRK-held territory; and that there was no military purpose behind them. Moving to unscheduled incidents, just to name two, Your Honours: Both originate from W-138. He testified about an air bomb incident on the 22nd June 1995, at Getoeva Street where a child died. The source is transcript 1212 until 1214. The second unscheduled incident, just as an example for Your Honour's consideration, is a shelling incident on a bus on the 18th of September, 1995. The transcript reference is page 1326, also in this relation Prosecution Exhibit 147. The third category of evidence, overview evidence of general nature, my colleague Mr. Docherty already mentioned witnesses Harland, Turkovic, Eva Tabeau, Overgard. I'm sure my colleague Ms. Edgerton will mention a few of them that relate both to sniping and also shelling. Just a few more examples, Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. Overgard testified, at page 636, that there was nearly daily shelling in Hrasnica at the end of 1995, a time, Mr. Tapuskovic this morning said, that nothing was really happening. We know from witness W-57, at page 4554, that Hrasnica was mainly civilian inhabited. Other witnesses who talk in general about the campaign of shelling was Azra Sisic, who came here to testify about Dobrinja. She said that water points were often targets for shelling in her area. That is page 2831. Also, other witnesses, Harland and also Ghulam Mohatarem, the brigadier from Pakistan who testified in the first week. They talked about what they called punitive shelling. My colleague Mr. Docherty already alluded to that. Basically, it means that shelling Sarajevo was meant to apply pressure to Bosnian government with no military purpose. Another quote for Mr. Mohatarem, at page 703, "Shelling was a regular process, but it would increase in intensity if the Serbs wanted to make a point, or if they were serving as -- they were facing reverses somewhere in any of those sectors, the shelling would intensify." Two more references, Mr. President, Your Honours, from our documentary evidence, especially from UN sources. P19, an UNPROFOR report of 2nd July 1995, and I quote: "The Serbs have resumed a more or less indiscriminate shelling of the city, adding that sniper activity has spread to a number of areas usually considered reasonably safe." The second example I would like to refer to, Your Honours, is Defence Exhibit number 9, again an UNPROFOR report, dated 24th June, 1995. It is very powerful, I suggest, Your Honours, and explicit document drafted by Mr. Harland saying: "Humanitarian situation bad. Civilians killed as Serbs shelled water lines and market places." Just ending up, Mr. President, Your Honours, only if you look at the scheduled incidents we have charged the accused with, they spread all over Sarajevo, starting from the bottom of any map, from the south-east with shelling incidents number 6 and 19 -- I'm sorry, in the south-west, starting with the shelling incidents number 6 and 19, going over Dobrinja, shelling incident number 14, then towards Novi Grad, shelling incident number 22, into the east, the old city, as an example, shelling incident number 5. So you can see in the territorial spread, it's all over Sarajevo, all over the urban part. In time, it's similar. We have used these incidents as an illustrative example, as you have been told consistently by the Prosecution. A brief word about the air bombs, Your Honours. We have led a lot of evidence, live evidence and also documentary evidence, including, very important, from these SRK documents with the signature of the accused that the SRK deployed air bombs. Air bombs, as you have heard many times, are inherently indiscriminate. Just a few quotes: Expert Zecevic, at 4851 and the next page; also David Harland talked about that at page 440; and also witness W-146. Two examples of the connection of air bombs to the SRK, the direct connection as you know, P225, exhibit of 7th April, 1995, with the SRK commander, the accused confirming in a regular combat report that he indeed used this bomb over civilian areas, and the second example is P226. Lastly, Mr. President, Your Honours, as Mr. Whiting already said, the Prosecution doesn't deny there was an ongoing war, but there is enough evidence, and a very good example is Ghulam Mohatarem, that the SRK shifted, shifted its tactics from engaging in normal war into targeting the civilians. And a very good example is at page 712 and 713 when, in relation to an attack of the SRK on 16 and 17 May, 1995, on Debelo Brdo, the SRK initially mounted a military campaign; and then when then saw they couldn't achieve it, totally abandoned it and started to indiscriminately shell the civilian part of Sarajevo causing many casualties. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has led evidence to show that there was a protected campaign in time, locations of the civilian population in Sarajevo conducted by the SRK under the command of the accused. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It's obvious now that I will be addressing, Your Honours, on the remaining count, 1, which charges the accused in this case with the crime of terror as a violation of the laws or customs of war. Our submission with respect to this count, Your Honours, is that the combined evidence which has been put before you in this case does demonstrate the existence of a campaign of shelling and sniping, and that it was a campaign which was designed, intended, and implemented to terrorise the civilian population of Sarajevo. It was the SRK which realised that campaign, and Your Honours have heard repeated evidence that the campaign did in fact cause terror. There's been evidence which shows the campaign was widespread and occurred over a long period, specifically from only weeks after the outbreak of war in and around Sarajevo in the spring of 1992. In that regard, I'd refer to Your Honours to Martin Bell at pages 5239, lines 4 to 5240, line 7; Harland, 323, lines 4 to 12 and 324, lines 11 to 19; and General Karavelic at page 4219, line 1 to 5. The campaign, Your Honours, continued throughout the indictment period and actually intensified in spring of 1995, and the references in this case would be to Harland, at 327, lines 11 -- 10 to 11; 329, lines 15 to 24 -- sorry, lines 15 to 33; 334, lines 7 to 24; Bell at 5240, lines 8 and own ward; 5244, lines 3 to 9; and P625, under seal, at page 27 of the English translation. This campaign, Your Honours, was firmly in place when the accused assumed command of the SRK in August of 1994; and by that time, its consequences were known not only locally but internationally. Significant witnesses have provided direct evidence in this case, Your Honour, that terror was the primary purpose of the campaign by the SRK: The Prosecution's first witness, David Harland; General Sir Rupert Smith; John Jordan; W-46; and W-158. I'd like to turn to that direct evidence first. David Harland testified that the specific purpose of the siege of Sarajevo was obvious to him for two reasons: First, the Bosnian Serb leaders specifically told him so. They said to him they used the shelling and sniping of Sarajevo to apply pressure, as my friend Mr. Docherty has said, on the Bosnian government that would force them to a peace agreement on terms that would be acceptable to the Serbs. Shelling and sniping, waging what Harland called a war of terror against the civilian population, "was a way," he said, "for the Bosnian Serbs to get had a we wanted." In that regard, I'd refer you to pages 324, lines 2 and onward -- sorry, 324, line 2 to 325, line 17; and 327, lines 5 to 22. Second, "the purpose of the campaign," Harland testified, "was manifest in the military behaviour of SRK forces." Most of the military activity, he reported on, wasn't conventional force on force military activity, but undirected or semi-directed artillery fire against civilian inhabited areas of Sarajevo. "This application of force," he said, "was purely then for the objectives of the application of terror against the civilians," and that as at pages 324, lines 23 over to 325, line 2; and 326, line 20 to 327, line 1. "This application of the instruments of terror," as Harland said, "was the principle activity of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps." "It was," he said, "what they did," and that's at 325, lines 14 to 18. Further, he said, "one could easily detect patterns of increase in the application of terror by the Bosnian Serbs through increased room random bombardment of the city, sniping, or cutting off the food supplies at times when they wanted to achieve greater political leverage." He used the analogy of a tap. "The amount of terror," he said, "was linked to the SRK military efforts." "The Serbs," he said, "had a spigot of terror. " And while the extent tent to which it was opened or closed varied. Throughout the course of the war, dynamic was the same. "The Serbs," he said, "intended to inflict maximum suffering on the people of Sarajevo, to induce their state authorities to agree to peace on their terms." But they were careful not to apply too much pressure, and he noted this dynamic continued through to October 1995. I'll refer you to pages 325, lines 2 to 13; and the same page, 325, lines 23 through to 326, line 19. Harland recalled, by way of illustration, words used by Radovan Karadzic on one occasion, which struck him. And they, to his mind, were among the factors that confirmed that the Serb intention was necessarily to starve the city but to inflict terror on its population. Discussing the Dobrinja-Butmir tunnel, "Karadzic," Harland said, "said that the Serbs could destroy it but they were going to let the Muslims breathe." "They could have," Mr. Harland testified, "cut off all the food and water and actually force the surrender of Sarajevo at certain points." But he noted they chose not, and they chose to allow the existence of the tunnel, at page 375, lines 9 to 16. Now, other witnesses gave similar evidence as to the primary purpose of the campaign from their own observations and perspective. General Sir Rupert Smith stated that with the exception of countering a specific military attack, he had no doubt that the purpose of campaign of shelling and sniping was to terrorise and to hold the pressure of Serb pressure in the minds of people on a daily basis. "It was," he said,"very effective, particularly on the ordinary run ever life in Sarajevo," and that's at pages 3311, line 7 to 22. I'd now, Your Honours, like to refer witnesses who testified in closed session; so if we could move into private session for that purpose, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness, John Jordan, volunteer firefighter and many other things for the civilians of Sarajevo: John Jordan's assessment of the deliberate nature of the campaign to terrorise Sarajevo civilians was articulate; and for this purpose, I'm going quote from his statement, which is P267, paragraph 42. He said: "What excuse can there be for shooting a firefighter when he is trying to put out a residential fire? What reason can there be for shelling water lines, bread lines, places with no military purpose? I can't remember a time when we weren't picking up wounded and dead people. The thing I noticed about certain attacks was that Serb shooters would go after the youngest in the family. If an adult and child were walking together, the child would be shot. If a family was walking, it would be the youngest. In a crowd of girls, it is seemed that the most attractive would be shot." It seemed that there was something very personal, almost grudge attacks doing whatever would cause the most pain to survivors. Your Honour, in our submission, there's ample evidence that as a result of the campaign, civilians in Sarajevo had no sense of security. Virtually no place in the city was entirely safe, and I would refer Your Honours to the testimony of Bell at 5242, lines 11 to 15; the testimony of Karacic in regard in part to sniping incident number 8 at 1185, lines 24, to 1186, line 4; Witness 121, page 2833, lines 13 to 20; and Witness Jasarevic at page 3004, lines 11 to 24. Travelling outside the house to get water was a risk. Water lines and water pipes were targeted. Snipers would sometimes even shoot at water containers and people that were carrying them. People would line for water between 2.00 and 3.00 a.m. to avoid being targeted, and the reference in that regard is Bell pages 5259, lines 18 to 23; P618; P295; paragraphs 19 to 23. Movement made people a target. People risked their lives every time they went out; and, again, I'd refer Your Honours to pages 1657, line 15 to 1658 line 3; W-62, lines 882 -- pardon me, page 882, lines 8 to 15; and P211. I'll talk briefly now, Your Honours, about three arms of the Prosecution's case, beginning with sniping. Your Honour, I will have to ask for movement in closed session for one last time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Closed session. Private.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Private, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. This was echoed by sniping expert Patrick Van der Weijden in P514 at page 7. He said that, "In a sniping, a victim killed by a sniper only affects the victim and people in the direct vicinity; but in the case of sniping, the thought of never being safe from the enemy affects everybody. Apart from being shot at, the anxiety mainly comes from not knowing where or exactly when the sniper will strike." General Fraser also confirmed that sniping had a major psychological effect on the population. Martin Bell testified -- pardon me, the reference in that regard is 1813, lines 18 to 24. Martin Bell testified that civilians even established rat runs to safely move from one place to another because sometimes it was unsafe to even go out of their front door. That's at pages 5243, lines 4 to 10, and P610. Trams were targeted. The Sarajevo tram system, Your Honours have heard, was symbolic of the normal functioning of the city. They stopped working in 1992 and resumed again in 1994. The hope was that when the trams resumed, things were getting better, but they too were hit. Page 5249, line 6 to 5250, line 10, and P614. Brigadier General Fraser described trams as a favourite target of snipers inside of Sarajevo because of the psychological impact it had on the people of the city. Shooting a tram gave shudders to the city and it meant that the situation was grave again. Page 1793, lines 18 to 24. Witnesses described their fear, the suspense of not knowing whether you were going to be shot and whether you might be injured, prevailed throughout the war. Pages 1658, line 24 through to 1659, line 15, and P92, refer. Moving on to shelling, you've already heard from my colleague Mr. Waespi that it was indiscriminate, unpredictable and for some witnesses a regular feature of their lives. I direct Your Honours to P185, page 3, P280, page 2, and P164. The pattern of artillery around Sarajevo, David Harland described, was one of dispersion of fire. Shells would be dropped apparently randomly across densely populated civilian areas of the city. While they might be concentrated in one area or another, they were not concentrated against military targets. Harland stated that they assumed one of the reasons for this was to keep the general level of terror high. Page 330, line 10, through to 331, line 18. Brigadier Higgs testified that with respect to the incidents he analysed, in particular, SS 2 at pages 5035 to 50346. And SS 23 at 5030, lines 8 to 24, he concluded that the rounds fired had no military objective and the only objective could have been to cause civilian casualties and put terror in the minds of the people in the areas of those incidents. A number of military officers in addition to other witnesses have described air bombs to Your Honours. One, General Fraser, aptly described them as a makeshift weapon with no military value. This officer, who had experience at all levels of military command, including artillery command, said he could never imagine a battlefield situation which would call for the use of a weapon like that. It had a huge explosive capacity and was psychologically devastating for the people. And that's General Fraser, lines -- pages 1825, line 22 through to 1827, line 12. Echoed by Knustad, at page 1992, lines 1 to 15; Overgard in respect of SS6, page 643, line 20, to 644, line 5; and P345, paragraph 23. Your Honours, on -- you've received evidence that on April 6th, 1995 the accused issued an order to the Ilidza Brigade to prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and transport the bomb for launching directed to the most profitable target in Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija and the order reads: "Where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted." That's P226. An air bomb did land in Hrasnica on the 7th of April, leveling five houses and causing one death. P621, and also P279 through to 282. Forensic investigator Hasanefendic, in respect of SS22, described the air bomb's primary purpose as massive destruction and intimidation; 2326, line 17 to 21; and Martin Bell described the air bombs as by their very nature weapons of mass destruction. "We might even call it," he said, "a weapon of shock and awe," at page 5262, line 6 to 11. Your Honours, the totality of the evidence you've received at this point in the trial in the Prosecution case shows these attacks, the attacks of this campaign were not militarily significant. You've received evidence to the effect that they were not so intense as to show a concerted attempt to take over the city. In fact, the attacks, in our submission, Your Honour -- and you have ample and, one would submit, substantial evidence in that regard -- the attacks passed one message to the people of Sarajevo: No one in the city was safe. And those are my submissions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Finally, I will address the individual responsibility of the accused and specifically focus on the evidence of command and control of the accused and his 7(3) responsibility. As Your Honours are aware, the accused is charged in each count with essentially four modes of liability: With planning, ordering, aiding and abetting, and with 7(3) responsibility, failure to prevent, failure to punish. In our submission, taking together the evidence -- the overwhelming of evidence of a campaign of shelling and sniping of civilian objects plus a campaign to cause terror, which has been already presented to you, put together with the also overwhelming evidence of the accused's command and control over the SRK, that that supports substantially all of the modes of liability, all four modes of liability that are charged with respect to each count. Now, with respect to command and control, point number one is that the evidence shows that the accused had effective command and control over the SRK and that he was an effective commander. I would point first to the testimony of General Fraser, transcript reference is 1784, 1810 to 1811, and 1818. I'll quote from 1818. General Fraser said: "Yes, Mladic was the boss, yes, he had significant control and command because he was directing operations not only in Sarajevo but for the rest of the country. But within that little box called Sarajevo, General Milosevic was the guy in command." There's also evidence from David Harland at transcript 337. He said: "We thought that the command and control, particularly on the Serb side, was very strong." David Harland said at transcript 353 that the accused was: "Was a forceful and commanding personality, rather more commanding presence, perhaps, that his predecessor, General Galic." There was also evidence -- and this evidence in fact was elicited by the Defence from Colonel Dragicevic, and this actually reminds me to make a point that I had intended to make at the beginning, which is that in our submission, the Defence has not disputed any of the evidence led by the Prosecution through numerous witnesses that the accused had effective command and control over the SRK. We in fact believe that the record shows that this -- because of their failure to challenge this evidence, as required by Rule 90 H, that this has in fact been conceded. Colonel Dragicevic said at transcript 4025 and 4010 and 3989 that the accused was a hands-on commander, that he spent a lot of time in the field, and that the SRK had superior "combat morale and strict military discipline." John Jordan testified at paragraph -- in paragraph 41 of his 92 ter statement, which is P267, and also viva voce at transcript 2645 that he went to Lukavica and saw the command -- the corps headquarters there approximately six times and he observed that it "seemed like they had good organisation and command structure." There's also evidence on the effective command and control from Major Eimers at 4789 to 90, and General Rupert Smith at transcript 3418 and from Exhibit P625 under seal at page 8. Secondly, there is evidence that protests to the corps command and requests to, for example, stop firing or to allow individuals to go through Serb checkpoints, that those requests made to the corps command were effective, that they were effectively implemented and very quickly, demonstrating an effective command and control structure at the corps level. I would refer Your Honours to General Fraser on this point at transcript 1771 to 1772; John Jordan, again, in his statement, P267, at paragraphs 15 and 32. He also testified live about this at 2635. He also talked -- John Jordan talked in paragraph 40 of his statement about getting permission to go through checkpoints, Serb checkpoints, and how was that effectively done. Major Eimers testified at transcript 4787 to 88 that when the UNMOs wanted firing to stop, they would contact Lukavica and the firing would typically stop within minutes. Major Eimers also talked about checkpoints at 4791. The next point is that there's evidence that orders were effectively passed down from the supreme command, the level of Mladic, and then implemented under the command of Dragomir Milosevic. And I -- I need to ask that we go into private session at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Colonel Dragicevic testified about how orders came down from the Supreme Command and that the accused would implement those orders and pass them on and make them orders of his own. He directly witnessed this, this happening and that evidence is at transcript 4056, 4067. There is further evidence about orders coming from the Supreme Command and being implemented effectively by the accused from General Rupert Smith, and those transcript references are 3298 to 3302. The next point is that there is evidence, substantial evidence from numerous witnesses that shelling and sniping in particular were controlled at the corps level. And again I'm going to have ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to return to the point about shelling and sniping being controlled at the corps level, there was also evidence about this from General Fraser at transcript 1773; Brigadier Ghulam Muhammed at transcript 704, General Rupert Smith at 3318 to 19 -- no, sorry, 3318 to 21; and from Mr. Higgs at transcript 5005 to 5006. The next point briefly is: There is also evidence which just reinforces this evidence that I've already spoken about that there no rogue elements within the SRK. That evidence came from several witnesses, including Brigadier Ghulam Muhammed at transcript 708; from John Jordan at paragraph 47 of his statement in evidence, which is P267; and from Major Eimers at exhibit P585, paragraph 37. We have, of course, in evidence numerous orders of the accused. I'll just cite a few of them: P390, P395, P396, P42, P3, P208, P225, P226, D141, P490, plus all of the orders that were put into evidence yesterday through witness Barry Hogan. In our submission, all of that evidence taken together shows that the accused had effective command and control and it can be inferred from all of the evidence that he planned, ordered and aided and abetted the campaign of shelling and sniping and of terror alleged in all of the counts of the indictment. Finally, Your Honours, the final point I will address is the 7(3) evidence of failure to prevent and punish. The first point to make with respect to this is that of course the -- there is substantial evidence that the command of the SRK and the accused were aware of the -- what was occurring in Sarajevo, what was being done by the SRK, aware of the campaign of shelling and sniping and of terror. This was something that was known, frankly, around the world. And it was certainly known by the command. Specifically, there is substantial evidence of many, many protest letters that were sent to the accused and to the command. Some of the examples of protest letters are P18, P28, P29, P30, P31, P32, P33, P36, P87, P101, P102, P103, P204, P343, and P392. General Nicolai testified, at transcript 937, that he wrote over 50 protest letters, and that most of the time the response to the protest letters were just denials or justification. That is at transcript 950. The second point on 7(3) is that, of course, the VRS had laws in place stating that commanders had a duty to initiate proceedings when there was a violation of the laws of war, and law is set forth in Exhibits P474 and P475, and there is evidence about how they were applied at transcript 3972 to 3973. There is evidence that there were no investigations; not even any investigations, let alone prosecutions, of invitations of the laws of war, even though many other crimes such as threats, dereliction of document, or other kind of domestic, violent crimes were investigated during this time-period were effectively prosecuted. I would refer Your Honours to the evidence P476 through P488. Those are the reports of investigations and prosecutions from December 1994 to October 1995, showing all of these other crimes that are investigated and prosecuted and not a single investigation for violations of laws of war. There are other reports in evidence which refer to the importance of discipline within the SRK for other matters. I refer Your Honours to P491, P489, D141, and P490. Colonel Dracigovic testified, of course, that there were no investigations or prosecution for war crimes during the indictment period. That's at T3983. This was also echoed by Major Eimers in P595 at paragraph 46. As I stated at the beginning, Your Honours need only find that there is sufficient evidence with respect to one alleged mode of liability for each count. We submit that all four modes of liability, which are alleged in each count, have been supported by substantial evidence, certainly sufficient for this Rule 98 bis proceeding. Unless there are any specific questions with regard to any of the counts or any of the points that have been made by the Prosecution, we will end our submission on that note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything in reply, Mr. Tapuskovic? You're not obliged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have noted down a lot of things. It would take a lot of time for me to respond to these submissions. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
