utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will now give the decision of the Trial Chamber on the Defence submission on under Rule 98 bis. Prior to its amendment in December 2004, Rule 98 bis B read: "The Trial Chamber shall order the entry of judgement of acquittal on motion of an accused, or proprio motu, if it finds that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction on that or those charges." Following the amendment, the rule now reads: "At the close of the Prosecutor' case, the Trial Chamber shall, by oral decision, and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties, enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. "The amendment was designed to achieve greater expeditiousness in the operation of the Rule. It did this in three ways: First, as this distinct from the former practice, there is no longer a written motion for acquittal with an oral submission, and the Trial Chamber gives its decision orally." Secondly, the new formulation clarifies that a judgment of acquittal is to be entered if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. But this had always been the standard, and this is confirmed by the following dicta from the Appeals Chamber in Jelisic. The Appeals Chamber held that the test for determining the applicability of Rule 98 bis is whether there is evidence, if accepted, upon which a Tribunal of fact could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused on the particular charge in question. The Chamber went on to say that thus the test is not whether the trier of fact would in fact arrive at a conviction beyond reasonable doubt on prosecution evidence, if accepted, but whether it could. Thus, as long as there is some evidence capable of supporting a conviction, a motion for judgement of acquittal will fail. One can look at the Mrksic judgement, which was referred to by the Prosecutor, for support for this proposition. The search for some evidence capable of supporting a conviction will in most cases be carried out more easily and more quickly than an examination into whether there is sufficient evidence to support a conviction. Rule 98 bis is based on the law and practice in common law jurisdictions relating to what is called a no case to answer submission. In keeping with that law and practice, the Tribunal's case-law makes clear that an acquittal at the end of the case is perfectly consistent with a Trial Chamber's rejection of a Rule 98 bis submission; that is, a decision that there is evidence capable of supporting a conviction. Significantly, the test proceeds on the basis that the Prosecution case is accepted, and, therefore, as Mr. Tapuskovic himself mentioned in his submissions, at this stage, the Trial Chamber is not concerned about contradictions or inconsistencies in the Prosecution's case, or, more generally, with issues of credibility. Those are matters to be addressed by the Trial Chamber in determining the guilt of the accused at the end of the case. Now, thirdly, and this is the third way in which the amendment achieved expeditiousness, the new rule clarifies that a judgement of acquittal relates to a Count in respect of which there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. If a Count is comprised of several parties, and there is no evidence on one part of the Count, the submission will fail, if there is evidence capable of supporting a conviction on the other parts. The Prosecutor has said as much. But this aspect of the new Rule is, in the Chamber's view, far from satisfactory. The Rule would seem to require, in the example given, not only that the submission should fail, but also that the one part of the Count, which has found to be not supported by any evidence, should also remain because the Count has survived. In the view of the Trial Chamber, this result is unnecessary and impractical. The survival of the Count should not oblige the Trial Chamber to retain for consideration, at the end of the case, a segment of the Count that it has found to be unsupported by any evidence. Moreover, such a result defeats one of the purposes of the Rule; namely, expeditiousness. A consequence of the Rule, and this would also have been the case with the former Rule, is that because charges in indictments at the Tribunal are, what I call, typically multi-layered, there is not much prospect for success for a Rule 98 bis submission. It is not unusual to find in an indictment, in the Tribunal, a Count charging a crime, such as a crime against humanity, with several, perhaps as many as 15 to 20, grounds. Thus, a Count could have as many as 100 or more separate allegations. It could cover 40 municipalities, be allegedly completed by 15 different mean, details of which could be set out in 50 or more items in a schedule. If there is some evidence on one of these grounds and none on the others, the submission will fail. Even if no further evidence is adduced in relation to those parts which the Chamber has found to be unsupported by evidence, it will be obliged to retain, to consider, and, at the end of the case, make a determination on them. Charges in indictments at the domestic level are generally not as multi-layered as they are at the Tribunal. A possible exception to this may be cases of fraud. Rule 98 bis, if it is to have any meaning, should reflect this difference; if it does not, the Rule is virtually devoid of any practical application at the Tribunal and serves very little purpose. The Chamber has not been able to find a case in which a motion or submission for acquittal has been successful in respect of all counts. Admittedly, it may be difficult to determine the extent to which the general multi-layered nature of the indictments accounts for this lack of evidence. However, at a minimum, the Rule should be amended to make it clear that if there is no evidence capable of supporting a part, a segment, a particular, or item of account, that part should be discarded at the halfway stage, while the rest of the count that is supported by evidence remains. As presently formulated and applied, a submission leading to the acquittal of the accused or of an accused at the end of the Prosecution case is only likely to succeed in the very rare case when the Prosecution case, as a whole, has broken down, so that there is no evidence of either the actus reus or mens rea of a crime. When one considers that the rational for the Rule in the until common law system is to ensure that at the end of the Prosecution's case, the jury is not left with evidence that cannot lawfully support a conviction, thereby preventing it from bringing in an unjust conviction, one must question the justification for the application of the rule in a system in which the Tribunal of fact is not only a person but a professional panel of Judges. Nonetheless, if there is need to find a justification for the retention of the Rule, it would have to lie in the possibility. It affords the accused to gain his or her freedom at the end of the Prosecution's case. I turn now to the submissions made. The gravamen of the Defence submissions is that the Prosecution was, and here I quote ,"completely unable to prove that there was in existence a campaign throughout the relevant period to target only civilians and civilian targets." It also submitted, that is the Defence, that there was no evidence to prove that the accused knew or had reason to know of the crimes committed by his subordinates. In that regard, the Defence completely rejected the Prosecution thesis of an inherited campaign and the inferences the Prosecution was asking the Chamber to draw from that. The Defence argued that the adjudicated facts from Galic were irrelevant to the criminal responsibility of the accused. The Prosecution, in its reply, made detailed submissions pointing to the evidence which it had led to support a conviction in respect of each of the seven counts. I turn now to an analysis of the evidence, and I make two things clear at the outset: First is that the conclusions arrived at are based on the analysis of the law that the Trial Chamber has carried out. Secondly, there has been no challenge to the Prosecution's case that there existed an armed conflict in Sarajevo at the relevant time. I also make it clear that the evidence on which the Trial Chamber will rely and to which it will advert for its decision includes the evidence referred to in the Prosecution's submissions, and this applies to all the counts. So let us look at Count 1, which charges the accused with the crime of terror as a violation of the laws and customs of war, punishable under Article 51 of Additional Protocol I, and Article 13 of Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions, and Articles 3, 7(1), and 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute. It is alleged that the accused planned and ordered, or in the alternative, aided and abetted the crimes charged in the indictment, and that he had criminal responsibility for the crimes as the commander of the perpetrators of those crimes. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence from a number of witnesses, including David Harland, Louis Fortin, and Thomas Knustad. David Harland testified on the 19th of January that shells were dropped by the Serbs apparently randomly across densely populated civilian areas in a way that would cause a small number of casualties in a large number of places. It was assumed by UNPROFOR personnel that this was to keep the general level of terror high and to forestall any dramatic events around which an international response would coalesce. Bogdan Vidovic testified that Martindvor, and in particular -- I misread that. He testified that Marindvor, and in particular an intersection in Marindvor, were under constant sniper fire, originating from positions of the VRS including from the Metalka building. Other witnesses have testified that the several areas in Sarajevo -- that several areas in Sarajevo were under constant sniper fire from Serb-held positions, and that they would have to move carefully to avoid being shot. There is evidence that the locations from which snipers operated were under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or the SRK. Milan Mandilovic testified that the State Hospital was exposed to both shelling and sniping, and that all of the 12 floors of the hospital were impacted by artillery fire. The side of the hospital overlooking Mount Trebevic was hit the most. According to Bakir Nakas, from 1994 until 1995, the Kosevo Hospital and its compound were hit dozens of times by shells. There is also evidence that modified air bombs were used by the SRK to shell civilian areas or buildings of Sarajevo. In addition, the Trial Chamber received documentary evidence detailing attacks on civilians by way of shelling and sniping. Let us now turn to Counts 2, 3, and 4, which charge the accused with murder, a crime against humanity, for conducting a coordinated and protracted campaign of sniper attacks upon the civilian population of Sarajevo, killing and wounding a large number of civilians of all ages and sexes. Count 3 charges the accused with inhumane acts, again a crime against humanity; and Count 4 charges the accused with unlawful attacks on civilians. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence from a number of witnesses, including Sanela Dedovic, Witness W-35, and Witness W-62. The evidence of these witnesses indicates that sniping took place in several places around Sarajevo. Sanela Dedovic testified that when she was 12-years-old, she crossed a street near a feature called Sharpstone in the north-east of Sarajevo. She was shot at and was hit in the ankle by a bullet which ricochetted off the pavement. There is evidence that the Sharpstone feature was a position of the VRS. Witness W-35 recounted how Alma Kotuna was shot while she was travelling on a tram near the old town of Sarajevo. When the tram reached the Holiday Inn Hotel and the museum, she was shot in the leg. There is evidence that the tram had been shot at from a location where the VRS held positions. The bullet that hit Alma Kotuna in the leg severed an artery. There is also evidence of sniping in the west of Sarajevo. Witness W-62 testified that 14-year-old Adnan Kasapovic was shot dead on his birthday while trying to cross a passageway. There is evidence that he was shot from the Institute for the Blind in Nedzarici, a known sniper's nest of the Serb army. Let us now turn to Counts 5, 6, and 7. Count 5 charges the accused with murder, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(a), 7(1), and 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute, and this for conducting a campaign of artillery and mortar and modified air bomb shelling on to civilian areas of Sarajevo and upon its civilian population. It is also alleged that these attacks were deliberate and indiscriminate and/or excessive and disproportionate to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Count 6 charges the accused with inhumane acts, a crime against humanity; and Count 7 charges the accused with unlawful attacks on the civilians, a violation of the laws or customs of war. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence from a number of witnesses who testified as to how civilian areas in Sarajevo were shelled. These witnesses include Enes Jasarovic and Witness W-138. Enes Jasarovic testified as to how, on the 24th of May, 1995, a 250-kilogram modified air bomb hit the Safeta Zajke Street in front of number 43. Two people were killed, five people were injured in the explosion. Several buildings in the vicinity were severely damaged which, according to some evidence, is a characteristic of the explosive charge used. Enes Jasarovic also testified that another air bomb hit the transformer station on Majdanska Street, very near to Safeta Zajke Street. At the transformer station, a further two people were killed and four people were injured. There is evidence that the modified air bomb at Safeta Zajke Street was fired from the direction of Lukavica, and that the modified air bomb, which hit the transformer station came from the same general area. Witness W-138 testified about the shelling of the TV building in Sarajevo. On the 28th of June, 1995, one person was killed, 28 persons were injured when a modified air bomb struck the TV building. The air bomb had come from a westerly direction, and Rijalda Musaefendic testified that Ilidza lies to the west of the TV building. I turn now to some specific issues of liability under Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute. There is evidence that during the indictment period, the accused was the commander of the SRK, the area of responsibility of which encompassed Sarajevo. There is also evidence that one of the first actions he took as commander was participating in negotiations for an anti-sniping agreement with the ABiH and subsequently signing that agreement. According to Ghulam Mohatarem, UNMO protested at meetings at which the accused was present about the occurrence of sniping. There is also evidence that the accused had effective control over the troops sniping at civilians, and that he knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit the crimes and failed to take the necessary measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators. With regard to the shelling of Sarajevo, there is evidence that the accused planned and ordered the use of modified air bombs in attacks. There is documentary evidence that a protest letter was sent to him personally after shelling incidents. Finally, there is documentary evidence that the accused acknowledged that the SRK had shelled the TV building. In the Trial Chamber's view, the above-mentioned evidence is on the basis of the criteria previously discussed capable of supporting a conviction for the crimes charges in Counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. Accordingly, the Defence submission is dismissed. Is there any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour I do have one final matter to raise, and it's a kind of sad matter for me personally. This marks the end of my participation in the case. I am leaving to go back to the United States to take up other responsibilities there. I will be teaching, and I can take to you more about that later. But it's been a pleasure and a honour to represent the Prosecution in this case before Your Honours, and it is with a heavy heart that I leave the case at this stage. However, it's lifted a great deal because I'm going to be leaving it in the hands of Mr. Waespi. He will be in charge of the case from here on, and he also will be supported by the team that you see before you and other members of the team that have appeared before you. I have every confidence that together under the direction of Mr. Waespi that they will continue to lead the Prosecution in the manner that you will expect. So with that, I say good-bye to Your Honours and to Defence counsel, and I will following this closely from my new position in the United States. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Whiting, you really have taken me by surprise. I had no intonation at all. Of course, I'm not privy to what happens in the Prosecutor's office. I can only say on my behalf, and I'm sure I speak on behalf of the Trial Chamber, that we are very sorry to see you go. I think your participation in the case, the way you have led the Prosecution has been exemplary, and I take some comfort that you're moving to an area which I can call my greatest love; that is, teaching. And may I inquire what you will be teaching, or is that a secret?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, no. It is not a secret, but I don't want to make this about me. But I will be teaching law students how to be prosecutors both in terms -- I am going to be a clinical law professor at the Harvard Law School starting in September, and so I will be teaching about domestic prosecutions, but also starting a clinic and teaching about war crime prosecutions. So I will be trying to send my students here to get experience and teaching them about what is happening here and other Tribunals in the world, as well as prosecutions back home in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to hear that and the Chamber wishes you everything that is good in your new profession, and everything that have you done here leads us to conclude that you will be successful. I also wanted to commend you for the spirit of cooperation that you have promoted between the parties. It is certainly the best that I have seen in the eight to nine years that I have been trying cases at the Tribunal, and I'm quite sure that that spirit of cooperation will continue. Mr. Tapuskovic, I know, will see to that, and Mr. Waespi in his new role as leader of the Prosecution team. So, once again, we wish you Godspeed and great success in your teaching endeavours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much for your words. They mean a lot to me. I very much appreciate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thank you for presenting me with an opportunity to address you after having heard that Mr. Whiting will be leaving the case. On behalf of my entire team, I wish to express our gratitude and pleasure for having been able to cooperate with Mr. Whiting. Indeed, throughout proceedings, there were no communication problems concerning the task that we embarked upon, and I am rest assured that that spirit will stay with us for the rest of the proceedings. On behalf of my entire team, I wish him all the best in his teaching career, and I truly mean it. Therefore, I needn't say anything else. I wanted to ask something else, however, concerning the leave to appeal your decision on established facts. When can we expect such a ruling to be made because it will have an impact on the preparation of our case.

utterances.text: We will give that decision today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.text: Yes. The decision is in the affirmative, will be in the affirmative in respect of both parties. We will grant the certification.

utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if I could say thank you to the Defence counsel for their words, and the feelings are fully reciprocated. I also appreciated the cooperation, and I am sure that it will continue. Thank you.
